facts.title: Discovered by a student
facts.text: Nitrogen was isolated in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford, a Scottish physician and student of Joseph Black at the University of Edinburgh. He removed oxygen and carbon dioxide from air and found a residual gas that could not support a flame or animal life. He called it "noxious air," because mice placed in it quickly suffocated.

facts.title: The name means 'lifeless'
facts.text: The name "nitrogen" comes from the French azote, coined by Lavoisier from Greek roots meaning "without life," reflecting that the gas does not sustain breathing or combustion. The modern name was later built from "niter" (potassium nitrate) plus the suffix -gen, meaning "niter-forming." Several languages, including French and Russian (azot), still use the older name today.

facts.title: It rules the air you breathe
facts.text: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume, making it by far the most abundant gas in the air. Despite being all around us, the N2 molecule is so unreactive that most living things cannot use it directly. Every breath you take is mostly nitrogen that passes in and out of your lungs untouched.

facts.title: One of the strongest bonds in nature
facts.text: In N2 the two nitrogen atoms are held together by a triple bond, one of the strongest chemical bonds known, requiring about 945 kilojoules per mole to break. This extreme stability is why atmospheric nitrogen is so chemically inert at ordinary temperatures. Breaking that bond to make useful compounds takes enormous energy, which is the central challenge of nitrogen chemistry.

facts.title: The reaction that feeds billions
facts.text: In the early 1900s, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process to combine nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia (NH3) at high temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst. This Haber-Bosch process produces the fertilizers that now sustain roughly half of the world's food supply. It is often called one of the most important inventions of the 20th century, and Haber received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

facts.title: A building block of life
facts.text: Nitrogen is an essential component of amino acids, which form proteins, and of the bases that make up DNA and RNA. Without nitrogen there would be no enzymes, muscle, or genetic code. Although plants and animals cannot use N2 directly, specialized bacteria in soil and in the roots of legumes "fix" it into usable forms, anchoring the entire food web.

facts.title: It boils at minus 196 degrees
facts.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at about -196 degrees Celsius (77 kelvin) and is produced industrially by distilling liquefied air. Cheap and intensely cold, it is used to flash-freeze food, preserve biological samples and reproductive cells, and create dramatic fog effects. A spilled drop skitters across a warm floor on a cushion of its own vapor, an example of the Leidenfrost effect.

facts.title: The gas that makes you laugh
facts.text: Nitrous oxide (N2O), a compound of nitrogen and oxygen, was discovered to have anesthetic and giddy effects by Humphry Davy around 1800, earning it the nickname "laughing gas." It is still used today in dentistry and medicine for mild sedation and pain relief. The same gas is also a potent greenhouse compound and is used as a propellant in whipped cream cans.

facts.title: Lightning makes fertilizer
facts.text: The intense energy of a lightning bolt can rip apart the triple bond in N2, allowing nitrogen to combine with oxygen and form nitrogen oxides. Rain then washes these compounds into the soil as natural nitrates that plants can absorb. In this way thunderstorms quietly fertilize the land, a process that supplied usable nitrogen long before factories existed.

facts.title: It paints the polar skies
facts.text: Nitrogen atoms and molecules high in the atmosphere contribute to the aurora, glowing when struck by charged particles from the Sun. Nitrogen emissions add blue and deep red hues to the curtains of light, complementing the green and red produced by oxygen. Beyond Earth, nitrogen ice covers parts of Pluto and Neptune's moon Triton, where geysers have been seen erupting nitrogen gas.
